name: Helenio Herrera
scopeNote: Counted: Atletico Madrid (1949-06-23 to 1952-12-28 per a Wikipedia mirror seen only in a search summary; Lazio Stories says sacked in January of the fourth season), Barcelona (1958 to mid-1960; exact days not found, 1958-07-01 and 1960-06-30 are approximate) and Inter (first match 25 Sep 1960 per Tuttomercato/inter.it summaries; appointed summer 1960; left June 1968; day approximate). Style term used by sources: catenaccio, specifically man-to-man marking by four defenders plus a free libero (Picchi), 5-3-2 per SI; Mazzola and Sacchi say attacking football at first and counter-attacking after the early 1960s, so 'purely defensive' is a popular label that is only partly right. Excluded-spell years (1959, 1967, 1940, 1981) are partial. Quote dates 1960/68 mean undated utterance in the Inter years (attributed). Partial dates (seasons) used when days not found. Atletico Madrid has no verified tactical page read: only a goals-per-game figure (FourFourTwo). Excluded: Roma 1968-71 (Coppa Italia 1969, no recognisable new tactical period, and the only Roma-era evidence read is Capello/Peiro anecdotes), Sevilla 1953-56, Valladolid, Belenenses, Spain and Italy national roles (short, shared with club, no titles), Barcelona 1980-81 and French clubs.
openQuestions: Exact dates of Atletico (23 Jun 1949 - 28 Dec 1952 vs Lazio Stories 'sacked in January'), Barcelona and Inter spells not verified on a page read.
No tier A source (Coaches' Voice site: search returned none); UEFA pages were not accessible.
Suarez transfer to Inter: These Football Times says 1960, other sources say 1961.
Atletico Madrid 1949-52 and Barcelona 1958-60 tactics are barely covered (only dropping Kubala, goals per game, psychology).
Peiro quote on being benched mixes Inter and Roma; not used as verified.
Pressing and set-pieces: only the Liverpool 1965 free kick incident found; no pressing source.
Primary dated Herrera interviews: Kuper 1994 and El Grafico 1964 only; his books (Yo, Tacalabala, Fitzpatrick's HH biography 2026) not read.
Doping and referee-bribing allegations (Mazzola 2015 confirmation of pills) not covered in verified evidence.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: “To the Catalans, I talked: ‘Colours of Catalonia, play for your nation.’ And to the foreigners, I talked money,” Herrera told Simon Kuper ... “I talked about their wives and kids. You have twenty-five players, you don’t say the same thing to everyone.”

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: Antoni Ramallets, the goalkeeper, told Lowe: “He had files on everything. He could tell you about the parents of some Italian or German, what day he was born, everything.”

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: For the first leg, in the capital, Herrera dropped Kubala, and Barça lost 3-1. The return leg ended with the same score, meaning a 6-2 aggregate loss.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: In La Liga, Herrera delivered the title in his first season. ... In 1959-60, Barça reached the semi-finals and met Madrid, who were yet to lose in the competition.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: A new sense of discipline was immediately installed. Players would cross Herrera at their peril. No individualistic quality trumped the value of obedience. The forward Antonio Angelillo, who in 1958-59 had scored 33 goals in as many league games, was thrown out because of his unruly social life.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: Armando Picchi, a commanding sweeper, once challenge Herrera’s authority and was shipped out to AS Varese. The only idler to survive was Mario Corso, an ingenious left-footed winger, whom Herrera constantly tried to offload, but who enjoyed the admiration and decisive support of Moratti. A player who pleased Herrera more was Suárez.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: He embraced his players before kick-off, and held one-on-one meetings known as ‘confessions’. He hunted information that could strengthen his relationship with the squad, instructing his masseur to overhear football-related utterances aired when players were in for treatment. ... Once, a squad member told the press that “we came to play in Rome”, instead of “we came to win in Rome”. The player got suspended.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: Herrera cultivated what became known as the ritiro. They were no-nonsense training camps where players were locked up in hotels for days, surrounded by staff, pitches and equipment.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: When English forward Gerry Hitchens left the club, he said it felt like “coming out of the bloody army”. ... Hitchens, Suárez and Corso fell behind the group and arrived late at the base. They discovered that the bus had left, and were forced to make the six-mile journey back to Milan on their own.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: The tactic was catenaccio, but with vital tweaks. Giacinto Facchetti, an athletic former centre-forward converted into an adventurous left-back, wreaked havoc down the flank. In 1965-66, he scored ten league goals. Centrally played an uncompromising sweeper with an excellent long pass – Picchi – and two centre-backs, Aristide Guarneri and Tarcisio Burgnich. The entire right flank was occupied by Jair, a hard-running Brazilian winger. In midfield, Suárez pulled the strings from deep. Corso loitered on the left, while Sandro Mazzola ... played off the main striker.

sources.evidence: Facchetti, an athletic former centre-forward converted into an adventurous left-back

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: Giacinto Facchetti, an athletic former centre-forward converted into an adventurous left-back, wreaked havoc down the flank. In 1965-66, he scored ten league goals.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: Herrera explained his style: “A small number of short, very quick passes to get to the opposition’s goal in as little time as possible. There is almost no place for dribbling. It’s a tool, not a system. The ball always moves further, and more quickly, when there isn’t a player behind it.”

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: “When he first arrived, he played attacking football,” Sacchi said, according to Wilson. “And then it changed. ... He started playing with a libero, told Suárez to sit deep and hit long balls, and started playing counter-attacking football.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: Brera wrote that Herrera turned to catenaccio in sheer desperation after a poor start in the early 1960s.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: In midfield, Suárez pulled the strings from deep.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: Herrera’s side had lost 3-1 away to Liverpool and, before the return leg, according to Wilson, Bill Shankly had claimed an Italian journalist had told him: “You will never be allowed to win.” Inter won 3-0 in a game riddled with controversy. Corso scored directly from an indirect free-kick, while striker Joaquín Peirò intercepted the ball from Tommy Lawrence

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: Corso scored directly from an indirect free-kick, while striker Joaquín Peirò intercepted the ball from Tommy Lawrence as the goalkeeper tried to kick it out. Both goals stood.

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: “When I hear about Inter playing catenaccio, I have to say we played about six matches with catenaccio and 40 matches with attacking football,” Mazzola told FIFA.com. ... “we didn’t feel very comfortable and secure, and stayed back more.”

sources.title: The incomparable legacy of Helenio Herrera
sources.evidence: Herrera claimed his system was misunderstood, because others had copied it and left out several attacking principles. This is supported by Mazzola

sources.title: The triumph and tragedy of Armando Picchi and Gaetano Scirea
sources.evidence: A traditional back four was deployed, but with the natural attacking instincts of Facchetti given licence to patrol the entire left side of the pitch. The extra man was placed into the sweeper role behind the back four. Inter would play a man-to-man marking system and leave a spare player at the back to sweep up any opponent or through ball that was missed.

sources.title: The triumph and tragedy of Armando Picchi and Gaetano Scirea
sources.evidence: Picchi had all the technical and mental attributes needed and so he became Herrera’s libero, captain and voice on the pitch.

sources.title: The triumph and tragedy of Armando Picchi and Gaetano Scirea
sources.evidence: Inter won their first Serie A title in nine years in 1963, conceding just 20 goals in 34 games. ... His natural instinct to defend meant that he very rarely crossed into the rarefied atmosphere of the opposition’s half – just as his manager intended.

sources.title: The triumph and tragedy of Armando Picchi and Gaetano Scirea
sources.evidence: Picchi was defensively inclined to the core, but he could play. ... he liked to get the ball down and move it quickly. Even though the opponent’s half was seen as a no-go zone, the Livorno native enjoyed instigating attacks.

sources.title: The triumph and tragedy of Armando Picchi and Gaetano Scirea
sources.evidence: Inter only conceded five goals in nine games against the English, French, Yugoslav, German and Spanish champions. ... Inter took a 1-0 lead over Benfica after 42 minutes. ... Inter registered a defensive performance that came close to perfection against a brilliant Portuguese attack.

sources.title: The triumph and tragedy of Armando Picchi and Gaetano Scirea
sources.evidence: Herrera asked the player, “What did Picchi say?” The player replied, almost apologetically: “Up yours and up yours to Herrera as well.” Inter went on to win the game.

sources.title: The triumph and tragedy of Armando Picchi and Gaetano Scirea
sources.evidence: Picchi’s promise had caught the wandering eye of Helenio Herrera, who would tempt the full-back from the provincial side to Internazionale

sources.title: The triumph and tragedy of Armando Picchi and Gaetano Scirea
sources.evidence: Winning the title by four points, Inter were once again difficult to break down, conceding only 28 goals all season but uncharacteristically scoring 70.

sources.title: Great Calcio Sides - Grande Inter (Forza Italian Football)
sources.evidence: This involved Inter going ahead in a game before sitting back with each of Inter’s four defenders man-marking the opposition’s main attacking threat and a libero sitting behind the centre backs sweeping up any attacks that managed to break through the strong defence.

sources.title: Great Calcio Sides - Grande Inter (Forza Italian Football)
sources.evidence: He stamped his authority on the side instantly and was a strict disciplinarian. Players were not allowed to smoke, drink, eat unhealthily or stay out too late during the evenings. Herrera went as far as to send officials around to check on the players to make sure they were at home.

sources.title: Great Calcio Sides - Grande Inter (Forza Italian Football)
sources.evidence: Tarcisio Burgnich and the great Giacinto Facchetti ... were employed as the preferred full backs in this side, Aristde Guarneri was a fine centre back and Armando Picchi was employed as the classy, tough-tackling libero.

sources.title: Helenio Herrera: The Innovator Who Single-Handedly Changed the Beautiful Game (SI)
sources.evidence: Herrera's standard formation at Inter was 5-3-2, with four man-marking defenders and a single sweeper combining to stifle opposition moves and restrict their freedom on the ball.

sources.title: Helenio Herrera: The Innovator Who Single-Handedly Changed the Beautiful Game (SI)
sources.evidence: Herrera ensured there was greater flexibility for counter-attacks in his side, in the process creating a formidable team that was equally capable of suffocating opponents and putting them to the sword.

sources.title: Helenio Herrera: The Innovator Who Single-Handedly Changed the Beautiful Game (SI)
sources.evidence: Herrera boastfully said of opponents Celtic: "I doubt whether they would beat us in the final in Lisbon. After all, we only need one goal." The Scots won 2-1.

sources.title: Herrera's creative engine room: God, Freud and Yoga (FourFourTwo)
sources.evidence: At Inter, he managed a free-scoring side but won nothing and turned to a variation of catenaccio that relied on attacking full-backs or wing-backs.

sources.title: Herrera's creative engine room: God, Freud and Yoga (FourFourTwo)
sources.evidence: his Atletico Madrid team scored 2.76 goals per game between 1949 and 1952, while at Sevilla (from 1953 to 1956) and Barcelona (1958 and 1960) his side averaged 2.29 and 3.03 goals a game respectively.

sources.title: Herrera's creative engine room: God, Freud and Yoga (FourFourTwo)
sources.evidence: he would stick up signs around the dressing room which challenged players: “Why not be the best?”

sources.title: Herrera's creative engine room: God, Freud and Yoga (FourFourTwo)
sources.evidence: Inter’s ritiro in Portugal was so claustrophobic that many players couldn’t sleep. Herrera’s invention had been so successful that he had forgotten another of his maxims: “Avoid monotony in speeches, training and meals.”

sources.title: Helenio Herrera (FC Barcelona)
sources.evidence: He had a confrontation with Kubala, who was gradually losing popularity. In his second year, despite winning the League championship again, the team's aim to win the European Cup was frustrated after losing against Barça's eternal rival, Real Madrid.
